difficultyReason: The stimulus presents three data points in partial tension — antibiotic use correlates with resistance in one setting but not another, with a subgroup exception. The correct answer resolves this tension via a hedged, carefully scoped inference. Distractors include a too-strong causal claim, an opposite-direction trap, a plausible-but-unsupported worldly claim, and a scope-creep trap that overgeneralizes to all pathogens.
stimulus: Data from a network of regional hospitals show that wards with the highest rates of broad-spectrum antibiotic use tend to have the highest rates of antibiotic-resistant bacterial infections, with one notable exception: pediatric intensive care units (PICUs) in those same hospitals show no such correlation. In PICUs, antibiotic use rates vary widely, but resistant-infection rates remain uniformly low across all facilities surveyed. Infection-control specialists note that PICUs universally enforce hand-hygiene and barrier-precaution protocols far more stringently than other wards do.
questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Strict enforcement of hand-hygiene and barrier-precaution protocols may reduce resistant-infection rates enough to offset the effect of high antibiotic use in some clinical settings.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reducing broad-spectrum antibiotic use is the most effective strategy for lowering antibiotic-resistant infection rates in all hospital wards.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Antibiotic-resistant bacteria cannot spread among patients in settings where hand-hygiene protocols are strictly enforced.

choices.label: D
choices.text: PICUs have lower rates of antibiotic-resistant infections than other wards because their patients are younger and therefore less susceptible to resistant strains.

choices.label: E
choices.text: High rates of broad-spectrum antibiotic use are the primary driver of antibiotic resistance in hospitals worldwide.

explanations.correct: The PICU data show that even with variable and sometimes high antibiotic use, resistant-infection rates remain uniformly low — and the one distinguishing feature of PICUs is rigorous infection-control protocols. This strongly supports the hedged inference in A: strict protocols may offset the effect of antibiotic use in some settings. The hedge ('may,' 'some') respects the inductive, non-entailed nature of the inference.
explanations.A: Correct. This is the most defensible inference: the PICU exception is best explained by the one variable that distinguishes PICUs from other wards — stringent infection-control protocols — and the answer is appropriately hedged.
explanations.B: Too strong and mis-scoped. The stimulus shows that reducing antibiotic use correlates with lower resistance in most wards, but the PICU exception reveals that other factors can dominate. Claiming this strategy is 'most effective in all wards' ignores the exception and uses absolute language the stimulus doesn't support.
explanations.C: Too strong. 'Cannot spread' is an absolute claim; the stimulus shows only that resistant infections are uniformly low in PICUs, not that transmission is impossible. This is the dominant 'too strong' trap.
explanations.D: Plausible but unsupported. Patient age and susceptibility are never mentioned in the stimulus; this introduces outside reasoning not derivable from the information given.
explanations.E: Scope creep and relative/absolute confusion. The stimulus covers regional hospital data; extrapolating to 'hospitals worldwide' exceeds the evidence. Additionally, labeling antibiotic use as the 'primary driver' globally overstates what the correlation in non-PICU wards can establish.

difficultyReason: The stimulus presents an economic dataset with a counterintuitive divergence between two related indicators: consumer confidence rises while discretionary spending falls among a specific income bracket, with a temporal complication. The correct answer must navigate the tension without overclaiming causation or generalizing beyond the scoped group. Distractors exploit opposite-direction confusion, absolute language, and plausible-but-unsupported economic reasoning.
stimulus: A national survey conducted over three consecutive quarters tracked consumer confidence and discretionary spending among households in the middle-income bracket. Consumer confidence scores rose steadily across all three quarters. Discretionary spending, however, declined in the second and third quarters, despite the rising confidence scores. During those same quarters, both mortgage refinancing activity and personal savings deposit rates increased substantially among the same households. The survey excluded households in the top and bottom income quartiles.
questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: For at least some middle-income households, rising consumer confidence does not always translate into increased discretionary spending within the same period.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Consumer confidence is a poor predictor of discretionary spending across all income groups.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Middle-income households reduced discretionary spending because they were pessimistic about future economic conditions despite their reported confidence scores.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased personal savings and mortgage refinancing caused middle-income households to feel more confident about their finances.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Discretionary spending among households in the top and bottom income quartiles followed a similar pattern to that observed among middle-income households.

explanations.correct: The stimulus directly shows that confidence rose while spending fell for this group across two quarters. Answer A draws the appropriately hedged inference — 'for at least some' and 'does not always' — that the two indicators can diverge within the same period. This respects both the data and the scope of the survey.
explanations.A: Correct. The divergence between rising confidence and falling spending for the surveyed group directly supports this hedged inference. The qualifier 'at least some' and 'does not always' ensure the claim stays within what the data establish.
explanations.B: Scope creep. The survey explicitly excluded the top and bottom quartiles, so no inference about 'all income groups' is warranted. This is the classic scope-creep trap — applying a finding to a population larger than the one studied.
explanations.C: Opposite direction and unsupported. The stimulus says confidence scores rose, contradicting the premise that households were pessimistic. Introducing hidden pessimism beneath confident scores adds unsupported psychological reasoning.
explanations.D: Inverts the direction of support. The stimulus presents savings and refinancing as coinciding with the spending decline, not as a cause of confidence. This answer also asserts a causal relationship the stimulus does not establish.
explanations.E: Plausible but unsupported. The stimulus expressly excluded the top and bottom quartiles from measurement. Any claim about their spending pattern is beyond what the data can support.

difficultyReason: The stimulus presents linguistic fieldwork data in tension: a grammatical feature appears in unrelated language families but is absent in several languages within a family that typically exhibits it. The correct answer requires recognizing what the distribution pattern does and does not imply about language contact versus inheritance, while staying hedged. Distractors include a too-strong universalist claim, an opposite-direction inference about inheritance, a plausible typological claim unsupported by these data, and a scope-creep generalization.
stimulus: Linguists studying evidentiality — grammatical marking that indicates the source of a speaker's information — have documented the following: the feature appears in languages from at least six unrelated language families distributed across four continents. Within the Tibeto-Burman family, however, where evidential marking is considered a characteristic feature, three recently studied languages in geographically peripheral subregions entirely lack it, though they retain other hallmark features of the family. No documented cases of evidentiality emerging through language contact between unrelated families have been identified in the dataset.
questionStem: The statements above, if true, most support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Evidentiality can be lost in some languages even when that feature is typical of the broader language family to which they belong.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Evidentiality arises independently in unrelated languages and is never transmitted through contact between speakers of different language families.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Languages that lack evidential marking are more likely to be found in geographically peripheral regions than in central ones.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The presence of evidential marking in a language is sufficient evidence that the language belongs to the Tibeto-Burman family.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The three Tibeto-Burman languages lacking evidentiality are more closely related to each other than to other members of the Tibeto-Burman family.

explanations.correct: The three Tibeto-Burman languages demonstrate that a feature characteristic of a family can be absent in some of that family's members. Answer A captures this with appropriate hedging — 'can be lost,' 'some languages,' 'even when typical of the broader family.' This is the most defensible inference the data yield.
explanations.A: Correct. The Tibeto-Burman data directly support this: despite evidentiality being a hallmark of the family, at least three member languages have lost it. The hedged phrasing ('can be lost,' 'some') keeps the claim within the evidence.
explanations.B: Too strong. The dataset shows no documented contact-transmission cases, but 'never transmitted through contact' is an absolute universal claim that the absence of cases in one dataset cannot establish. This is the dominant too-strong trap.
explanations.C: Plausible but unsupported. The three languages are described as geographically peripheral, but the stimulus provides no comparative data on central languages' rates of lacking evidentiality. Concluding a general tendency from a single directional observation is unwarranted.
explanations.D: Opposite direction and too strong. The stimulus shows evidentiality across at least six unrelated families, making it clear that Tibeto-Burman membership is neither necessary nor sufficient to predict evidentiality. This inverts the logic of the data.
explanations.E: Plausible but unsupported. The internal phylogenetic relationships among the three peripheral languages are never discussed in the stimulus. Inferring closer relatedness among them introduces information not derivable from the facts given.
